lead: The 8085 is an 8-bit microprocessor. Inside, one 8-bit internal bus connects the ALU, accumulator, general registers, program counter, stack pointer, instruction decoder and control blocks. This single bus keeps the chip small and cheap, but it means only one byte moves at a time. The 40-pin package brings out a 16-bit address as two 8-bit halves and an 8-bit data bus that shares pins with the low address. Students meet it in lab kits, in old ticketing terminals and in every course that starts 8085 assembly.
prereq: You need: CPU, memory, buses and the stored-program idea from Unit 1, Foundations.

sections.h3: Internal blocks and the single bus

blocks.text: The 8085 is an 8-bit CPU. Every internal data transfer is 8 bits wide. The ALU does 8-bit arithmetic and logic. One ALU input comes from the accumulator (register A). The other comes from a temporary register that the programmer cannot name. The ALU writes its result back to A and sets the flag register. Some syllabi call this set of blocks the functional building blocks of the processor.

The programmer-visible registers are A, B, C, D, E, H and L. All are 8 bits. B-C, D-E and H-L can be used as three 16-bit pairs. The program counter (PC) is 16 bits and holds the address of the next instruction byte. The stack pointer (SP) is 16 bits and holds the top of the stack in memory.

The instruction register (IR) holds the opcode byte just fetched. The instruction decoder turns that opcode into control signals. Timing and control sequences the machine cycles and drives RD, WR, ALE and the status lines. Interrupt control handles the interrupt pins. Serial I/O control handles SID and SOD. The clock states inside each machine cycle are covered in 2.2.

Two buffers face the pins. The address buffer holds the high address byte A15-A8. The address/data buffer carries the low address byte AD7-AD0 in the first clock state, then carries data. Because address and data share pins, an external latch must hold the low address when ALE pulses.

The accumulator A is the centre of arithmetic. Most 8-bit results land in A. The flag register is also 8 bits, but only five bits are defined: S, Z, AC, P and CY. The other three bits are unused. A flag bit changes only when an instruction affects that flag.

items: S (sign): copy of bit 7 of the result. S=1 means the result looks negative in two's complement.
Z (zero): Z=1 when all result bits are 0.
AC (auxiliary carry): carry from bit 3 to bit 4. The decimal-adjust instruction DAA uses it.
P (parity): even parity. P=1 when the result has an even number of 1 bits.
CY (carry): carry out of bit 7 in addition, or borrow in subtraction.

blocks.text: Not every instruction changes every flag. MOV changes no flags. INR does not change CY. The full instruction-by-instruction flag table belongs to Unit 3, Instruction Set and Assembly Programming.

sections.h3: The 40 pins that face the outside world

blocks.text: The 8085 comes in a 40-pin DIP. Pin 40 is Vcc (+5 V) and pin 20 is Vss (ground). Pins 1 and 2 are X1 and X2 for the crystal.

items: Pins 21-28: A15-A8, the high address byte, output.
Pins 12-19: AD7-AD0, multiplexed low address and data.
Pin 30: ALE (address latch enable). It goes high in T1; its falling edge latches AD7-AD0 into an external latch.
Pin 32: RD active low. Pin 31: WR active low.
Pin 34: IO/M. 0 selects memory; 1 selects I/O.
Pin 29: S0. Pin 33: S1. These status pins identify the bus cycle.
Pin 35: READY input. A low level inserts wait states.
Pin 39: HOLD input. Pin 38: HLDA output. This is the DMA handshake.
Pin 36: RESET IN. Pin 37: CLK OUT. Pin 3: RESET OUT resets peripherals.
Interrupt pins: TRAP pin 6, RST7.5 pin 7, RST6.5 pin 8, RST5.5 pin 9, INTR pin 10, INTA pin 11 active low.
Serial pins: SID pin 5 input, SOD pin 4 output.

blocks.text: A15-A8 and AD7-AD0 together form the 16-bit address. During T1 the low byte is an address; after ALE latches it, AD7-AD0 becomes the data bus. DMA and interrupt priority are expanded in Unit 5, Peripheral Interfacing.

examples.question: The 8085 adds 9AH and 7CH. Give the accumulator content and the flag register bits S, Z, AC, P and CY.
steps: Add as 8-bit numbers: 1001 1010 + 0111 1100 = 1 0001 0110. The 9-bit sum has a carry out of bit 7, so CY = 1.
Keep the low 8 bits: 0001 0110 = 16H = 22 decimal. This is the new accumulator content.
S is bit 7 of 0001 0110. Bit 7 is 0, so S = 0.
Z is 0 because 0001 0110 is not zero.
AC uses the lower nibbles: A + C = 10 + 12 = 22 decimal = 16H. This is more than 0FH, so a carry passes from bit 3 to bit 4. AC = 1.
P is even parity. The result 0001 0110 has three 1 bits (bits 4, 2 and 1), an odd count, so P = 0.
The flag bits in order S Z AC P CY are 0 0 1 0 1.
examples.answer: A = 16H = 22 decimal; S = 0, Z = 0, AC = 1, P = 0, CY = 1.
examples.check:
a = 0x9A
b = 0x7C
total = a + b
low = total & 0xFF
cy = (total >> 8) & 1
S = (low >> 7) & 1
Z = 1 if low == 0 else 0
AC = 1 if ((a & 0x0F) + (b & 0x0F)) > 0x0F else 0
P = 1 if bin(low).count('1') % 2 == 0 else 0
print(low)
print(S)
print(Z)
print(AC)
print(P)
print(cy)

traps: AC is the carry from bit 3 to bit 4, not the carry out of bit 7. CY is the carry out of bit 7.
8085 parity is even parity: P = 1 only when the result has an even number of 1 bits. It is not odd parity.
AD7-AD0 is not a pure data bus. It carries the low address byte in T1. ALE and an external latch separate address from data.
IO/M = 1 selects I/O. Memory is selected when IO/M = 0.
A flag is not always updated. MOV changes no flags, and INR does not change CY.

quiz.q: Name the five defined bits of the 8085 flag register.
quiz.a: S, Z, AC, P and CY: sign, zero, auxiliary carry, parity and carry.

quiz.q: How wide are the 8085 program counter and stack pointer?
quiz.a: Both PC and SP are 16 bits wide.

quiz.q: Why does the 8085 need the ALE signal?
quiz.a: AD7-AD0 carries the low address byte in T1 and data later. ALE goes high in T1 so an external latch can hold the low address after AD7-AD0 switches to data.

quiz.q: Add 3CH and 45H in the 8085. Give A, CY, S, Z, AC and P.
quiz.a: 3CH = 0011 1100; 45H = 0100 0101. Sum = 1000 0001 = 81H, so A = 81H and CY = 0. S = 1, Z = 0. Lower nibbles C + 5 = 12 + 5 = 17, so AC = 1. 81H has two 1 bits, so P = 1.

quiz.q: A result has an even number of 1 bits. What is P and why?
quiz.a: P = 1. The 8085 uses even parity, so it sets P when the count of 1 bits in the result is even.

quiz.q: Why is AC not the same as CY? Use 9AH + 7CH as your example.
quiz.a: CY is the carry out of bit 7. AC is the carry from bit 3 to bit 4. In 9AH + 7CH, the low nibbles A + C give 16H, so AC = 1; the full 8-bit sum gives a 9-bit total, so CY = 1. They are separate carries.

quiz.q: Which 8085 pins carry the low address byte during T1, and what do they carry later?
quiz.a: Pins 12-19, AD7-AD0, carry the low address byte during T1. After ALE latches that byte, the same pins carry data D7-D0.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the 8085 survives in teaching kits and legacy equipment; modern designs use ARM Cortex-M or RISC-V microcontrollers. The same ideas—one internal bus, multiplexed pins and a flag register—appear in the 8051 and the 8086. Search for '8085 pin diagram', '8085 flag register' and '8085 ALE latch' for practice. The 8086 splits instruction fetch and execution differently; see 2.3.
